newsitem.title: DUBAI: Moslems to mark haj climax after fire kills 217.
newsitem.headline: Moslems to mark haj climax after fire kills 217.

text.p: Workers cleared the debris of a fire that gutted a Saudi tent city, killing 217 people and wounding about 1,300, as two million Moslems on Wednesday began the final stage of the haj pilgrimage .

Diplomats and Saudi authorities did not have new casualty figures from the blaze that had spread panic among thousands of pilgrims performing Islam's holiest duty as it engulfed 70,000 white tents in the Mena plain, 11 km (seven miles) from Mecca.
Saudi television said early on Wednesday the fire, which spread quickly in high winds, was extinguished in three hours. It put the official death toll at 217. Over 1,290 were injured.
There was no official breakdown of victims' nationalities.

Diplomats and witnesses said Tuesday's blaze had been caused by gas cylinder explosions. Television pictures showed security forces dragging gas cylinders from the site and wild flames racing across a sea of tents.
Saudi Arabia has not yet announced the cause of the fire.
Diplomats said Saudi authorities were still trying to identify victims, a difficult task as many bodies were charred beyond recognition.

"We do not have new casualty figures. We expect they will run into three figures," said Indian ambassador Mohammad Hamad Ansari. "It's hard to say because the bodies were charred in the fire and we cannot identify them except from a missing persons list which is difficult because all the pilgrims are on the move," he told Reuters by telephone from Mena.
"It could be one hundred, it could be more," he said of the number of Indian victims, which on Tuesday he put at 100.

Diplomats had said most victims were reported to be from India, Pakistan and Bangladesh. Saudi newspapers on Wednesday said the fire had also engulfed Syrian, Lebanese, Egyptian, Sudanese, Yemeni and Moroccan tents.
Asked about Pakistani victims, reported to be around 30, Pakistan's director of haj Ahmed Bakhsh told Reuters: "We don't know because the fire spread in so many areas."
Saudi television said the pilgrims started their journey from Mena to Mount Arafat, where Prophet Mohammad gave his last sermon 14 centuries ago, after dawn prayers on Wednesday.
Praying at Mount Arafat, commanding the Mena plain, marks the climax of haj. On Thursday, Moslems around the world celebrate Eid al-Adha (Feast of Sacrifice) at the end of haj.

The television showed a congested mass of pilgrims, carrying umbrellas to shield against the sun, making their way to Mount Arafat, chanting: "I have answered your call, God, there is no God but you."
The wide road from Mena to Mount Arafat was a white sea of pilgrims and helicopters flew through hazy morning skies. Saudi papers said sand storms were possible.

Diplomats said workers had started clearing debris and erecting new tents to receive pilgrims on their way back from Mount Arafat. Pilgrims will spend the night at Mozdalifah, between Mena and Mount Arafat, where they will stone three pillars symbolising the devil.
Newspapers said many pilgrims had not yet reached the tents when the fire broke out, preventing more loss of life.

Saudi Health Minister Osama bin Abdul-Majid Shobokshi said on Saudi television on Wednesday the quick response of civil defence and fire fighters had save many lives. "Many of the injured are in satisfactory condition. Many of them have already left hospitals," he said.
Witnesses reported women sobbing and dazed pilgrims trying to flee the fire or looking for missing relatives and friends.
The television said King Fahd had expressed condolences to the families of the victims. U.S. President Bill Clinton said in Washington he was deeply saddened.

The blaze was the latest tragedy to strike the pilgrimage to Mecca, Islam's holiest shrine. Able-bodied Moslems are obliged to make the haj at least once if they can afford it. In 1990 1,426 pilgrims were crushed to death in a stampede in a tunnel and in 1994 270 pilgrims died in another stampede.

Saudi Arabia, custodian of Islam's two holiest shrines, has spent $18.6 billion in the last decade on expanding pilgrimage sites and officials had said they were doing their best to ensure a safe haj.
